summary: The environment can start the sample build now: Python, pip, Docker, az, node, the documentdb MCP server, and a comprehensive set of documentdb-* skills are installed and a live DocumentDB cluster is reachable via the DOCUMENTDB_URI env var. Most cold answers were partially or wholly incorrect because they described Cosmos DB databaseAccounts, the older Cosmos vCore naming, Amazon DocumentDB, or generic MongoDB behaviours; the installed skills and Microsoft Learn pages provide the correct, current facts. Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and several optional CLIs are noted; several design choices remain unspecified (LLM provider/model, explicit customer schema, seed data), which the builder must decide before committing code.
summary_points: All essential runtime tooling for the Python/LangChain sample is present: python (3.13), pip, node, docker, az (signed-in), and the documentdb MCP server — the build can start.

Key factual cold-answer errors would break the sample if used (resource type, connection string form, billing model, local gateway port, AAD auth support, full-text/vector index semantics); these are corrected and grounded to skills/docs.
Installed documentdb-* skills (deployment, driver, connection, vector-search, full-text-search, natural-language-querying, etc.) provide most implementation guidance the builder needs.
One useful accelerator is missing: the DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — its absence slows agent-skill scaffolding but is not blocking.

Several non-blocking information gaps remain that the builder must decide: LLM provider/model, explicit document schema and collection names, sample-data seed script, and whether to use local gateway vs live cluster for tests.
No inventory tool is absolutely required and missing without workaround; the verdict is ready_with_gaps, not blocked.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource id: /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/<accountName>).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for this managed MongoDB-compatible offering: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API examples use the mongoClusters resource type and API-version 2025-09-01).
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment skill and Microsoft Learn 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' resource reference
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the older Cosmos DB Account resourceModel (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) used for Cosmos DB and for the Cosmos DB Mongo API (RU model). The new dedicated managed MongoDB offering uses a different resource type: mongoClusters.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts would lead the builder to generate ARM/Bicep that targets Cosmos DB databaseAccounts; deployments would either create the wrong service or fail to create the new mongoClusters resource. The sample would be wired to the wrong control-plane API and the MCP server calls may not find the cluster.
improvements: Add a prominent sentence on the main Azure DocumentDB quickstart page that 'this managed MongoDB product uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts)'.

Add a deprecation/clarification note to the Microsoft Learn page for Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts explaining the difference and linking to mongoClusters for vCore-based/mongoClusters offerings.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in (core) CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=westus --kind MongoDB. (No separate extension required in current az releases.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The deployment examples and recommended paths use az resource create with resource-type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters" and the documentdb Bicep/azurerm (or az resource) flows; there is also guidance for a dedicated az extension preview in some releases, but the canonical examples in the documentdb skill use az resource create / Bicep and the resource-type 'mongoClusters'. Do not rely solely on az cosmosdb database-account commands for the vCore/mongoClusters flow.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment skill and Microsoft Learn quickstarts

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the Cosmos DB az cosmosdb command group used for databaseAccounts (the RU-based Cosmos Mongo API). The vCore-managed mongoClusters resource is deployed via az resource / Bicep templates or provider-specific Az modules; the CLI group differs.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create creates or manages Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (RU model), not the vCore/mongoClusters resource; provisioning attempts or management scripts would target the wrong resource model.
improvements: Document the recommended az resource create examples for mongoClusters on the Quickstart page and add an explicit callout 'Do not use az cosmosdb for mongoClusters; use az resource with Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters or the supplied Bicep module.'

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-06-15' = { name: 'myAccount' properties: { kind: 'MongoDB' ... } }). Terraform: use resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB offering the Bicep/ARM resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (examples in the documentdb skill and referenced Bicep templates use that resource type and API version). Terraform uses azurerm_mongo_cluster (or the azapi/azurerm provider equivalent) targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment skill and referenced Bicep/Terraform templates
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the older databaseAccounts resource and the azurerm_cosmosdb_account Terraform resource (Cosmos DB RU model). The vCore-managed offering uses mongoClusters and the newer azurerm/azapi resources.
confusions.build_risk: Using the databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource shapes will create the wrong service type or fail for the vCore workflow; IaC generated from the cold answer won't match the cluster you must use.
improvements: Add a short 'Which resource to use' section to the Bicep/Terraform quickstarts showing both resource types (databaseAccounts vs mongoClusters) and when to choose mongoClusters for vCore-based DocumentDB.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style connection string. Example (TLS): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Host suffix: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com. TLS/SSL port: 10255 (the TLS/SSL MongoDB port for Cosmos DB Mongo API). Options normally include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings are SRV-style in recent examples. The documentdb skill shows mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (and for Microsoft Entra ID auth use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC). Do not assume port 10255 or the .mongo.cosmos.azure.com suffix — the vCore service uses cluster-specific hostnames such as *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or SRV records.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment skill and Microsoft Learn connection guidance

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the Cosmos DB Mongo API connection format and port (older RU model) rather than the SRV-style cluster hostnames used by the vCore/mongoClusters offering.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB MongoDB connection strings and ports (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong connection string format (wrong host suffix or port) will cause connection failures. The sample must read DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it verbatim to pymongo.MongoClient; it must not rewrite host/port assumptions.
improvements: Add an explicit example on the sample README showing the exact placeholder DOCUMENTDB_URI form (SRV) expected for the vCore/mongoClusters offering.
Document that the sample must accept either SRV (mongodb+srv://) strings or standard URIs as provided in the portal and must not hardcode ports.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is Azure Cosmos DB RUs (Request Units) + storage. You can provision throughput (RUs/sec) at database/collection level or use serverless (pay-per-request, where available). There are newer managed MongoDB-like SKUs in Azure that use instance sizes (M-series/vCore) for compatibility, but the common/Azure-native model is RU-based provisioned or serverless.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed offering) uses compute tiers with vCores (M-series tiers like M10..M200) and storage billed separately; it is not RU-based like Cosmos DB for NoSQL (RU model). The skill and docs highlight compute (vCore) + storage pricing for this service.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment skill and Microsoft Learn pages describing vCore tiers

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing + tiers)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixes Cosmos DB RU-based billing (the traditional Cosmos model) with the newer vCore M-series offering; historically Azure had RU and vCore flavors and their names overlap.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based throughput they may design the sample to call RU-scaling endpoints or include RU-specific client options; tests and cost estimates would be incorrect. The sample should assume vCore tiers and follow the documentdb-azure-deployment defaults (M30 for prod).
improvements: Add a short 'Billing model' blurb on the main quickstart page clarifying 'this service is vCore-based (M-series) — not RU-based Cosmos DB for NoSQL'.
Add a pointer on the pricing page that explains differences between RU-based and vCore-based MongoDB offerings.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API you normally authenticate with Mongo-style credentials (username/password) provided by the Cosmos DB account (SCRAM-style) or use the account connection string (account key) in the URI. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is supported for some Cosmos DB APIs (SQL/Table) via RBAC, but for the MongoDB API there is no general Azure AD-backed MongoDB driver authentication; drivers use the Mongo credentials/connection string. (If AAD support is required, use an API that supports AAD or a proxy.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM-style) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) via OIDC: clients can present Entra-issued OIDC tokens (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC or MONGODB-OIDC in URI) or use managed identities. Entra ID auth is enabled by toggling authConfig.allowedModes to include MicrosoftEntraID (the docs show sample SRV connection string with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn 'Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control' and documentdb-azure-deployment examples

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control (Entra/AAD OIDC)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API docs historically lacked AAD/OIDC support; the cold answer assumes that limitation. The vCore DocumentDB offering has explicit Entra/OIDC integration.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API auth guidance (no AAD)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra/AAD is unavailable they may ship long-lived passwords or keys; conversely, if they assume only AAD they may fail to include native credentials fallback. The sample should support reading a DOCUMENTDB_URI and also document how to configure and test Entra auth if the user wants it.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Authentication options' example to the quickstart that shows both native (SCRAM) connection string and the OIDC connection string and how to enable Entra auth on the cluster.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For apps use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. pymongo for Python). The MongoDB wire protocol compatibility means no service-specific application driver is required. For management tasks use the Azure management SDKs (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / az cli).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: applications should use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python). For management and provisioning use the Azure CLI/Bicep/Terraform flows or the documentdb deployment skill. There is no special application runtime SDK required for data-plane operations.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-driver skill and Microsoft Learn compatibility docs

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: If the cluster exposes vector indexes it uses algorithm types such as HNSW, IVF or DiskANN (service-dependent). The create-index pattern is non-standard to MongoDB and looks like a special vector index command. Example (best-effort concrete guess): db.products.createIndex({ embeddings: "vector" }, { algorithm: "hnsw", dims: 1536, metric: "cosine" }). Note: the exact index option names vary by service; confirm with the cluster's index API/management tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes via the cosmosSearch index type with sub-kinds vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, and vector-ivf. Indexes are created with a createIndexes/createSearchIndexes-style command using key: { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' } and a cosmosSearchOptions block including kind (vector-diskann/vector-hnsw/vector-ivf), dimensions, similarity, and other algorithm-specific options. Example usage and full parameter names are documented (createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions).
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-vector-search skill and Microsoft Learn 'Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB' pages

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer guessed a MongoDB-style createIndex signature (which is closer to Atlas examples) rather than DocumentDB's cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions createIndexes pattern.

confusion_sources.title: Atlas / community vector index examples (createIndex with custom 'vector' type)

confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create vector indexes using community MongoDB syntax will fail; the sample must use the documentdb-specific createIndexes/createSearchIndexes pattern and parameter names (cosmosSearchOptions).
improvements: Include a one-line example in the sample README showing the exact createIndexes JSON for a DiskANN/HNSW/IVF index on the sample collection (dimensions and similarity).
Document that vectors must be number[] and show how to store vector metadata (model name + dims) in the document.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Simple full-text search: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })). For richer/hybrid text+vector search integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or the service's vector-search feature (if available) which can combine text scoring and vector similarity. Cosmos DB does not automatically provide the same hybrid search features as dedicated search services—use Cognitive Search or the provider's vector-search extension.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB uses createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage for full-text search (BM25) — not the MongoDB community $text/index type. It also supports hybrid BM25 + vector retrieval natively (via createSearchIndexes and cosmosSearch operator) and provides rules for custom analyzers and hybrid ranking (Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Do not rely on community $text indexes for DocumentDB full-text search.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-full-text-search skill and Microsoft Learn 'Integrated search' docs
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumes community MongoDB $text indexes or an external search integration; Azure DocumentDB provides its own full-text and hybrid capabilities via createSearchIndexes and $search.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses $text indexes or relies on external Cognitive Search it will miss the more powerful built-in $search + cosmosSearch hybrid options or use incorrect operators; queries will fail or produce different results.
improvements: Add a 'search' quick example in the sample README showing createSearchIndexes and a $search stage projecting searchScore so builders don't reach for $text.
Mark clearly on quickstart that DocumentDB's search uses createSearchIndexes and is not the same as MongoDB $text.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported wire protocol versions depend on account configuration; recent managed accounts support MongoDB server versions up to 6.0–7.0 (e.g. MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol) depending on the SKU. Common unsupported or limited features vs upstream MongoDB: some admin/replica-set ops, direct oplog access, certain server-side JS ($where), unsupported or limited server commands, and some aggregation operators or behaviors may differ. Always check the account's supported server version and feature matrix before depending on advanced MongoDB features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and advertises ~99.03% operator compatibility; administrative server commands and some admin ops are intentionally abstracted by the platform. Builders should consult the compatibility matrix for operator-level details but can expect broad support (including many aggregation operators).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn compatibility docs and documentdb skills

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions list)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was conservative and under-specified on supported protocol versions; the service documents explicit 5.0–8.0 support.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a narrower subset of wire protocol versions may cause the builder to constrain feature usage unnecessarily; conversely, relying on unsupported admin commands will fail.
improvements: Add a clear 'supported wire protocol versions' line on the main docs for quick reference (5.0–8.0).

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full emulator for the MongoDB API of Cosmos DB. For local development run a MongoDB server (official image) to exercise the MongoDB driver compatibility: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:7.0 and connect via mongodb://localhost:27017. For Cosmos DB-specific behavior test against the real cluster (or use Azure Cosmos DB emulator for SQL API only).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) for local development exposing the MongoDB-compatible gateway port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). Use this Gateway image for local parity; the official MongoDB image is an acceptable fallback for pure-driver compatibility but will not emulate DocumentDB-specific features (vector indexes, RBAC, etc.).
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-local-deployment skill

grounding_links.title: Local gateway image and port guidance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated Cosmos DB's lack of emulator for its SQL API with the vCore DocumentDB offering's local gateway image; many blogs recommend using a plain Mongo container, which led to the misstatement.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB official image usage for driver compatibility (community guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses a raw MongoDB image for feature validation they will miss DocumentDB-specific features and tests (e.g., cosmosSearch, vector indexes, Entra auth). The sample should prefer the documentdb-local gateway image when local tests are required.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' note to the sample README that shows the exact docker run or docker-compose snippet for the Gateway image and port 10260.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams for the MongoDB API have historically been limited or unavailable. If you need change notifications on Cosmos DB use Cosmos DB Change Feed (SQL API) or check the account's MongoDB server-version compatibility for change-stream support. In short: assume change streams are not generally available unless your specific account version explicitly advertises support; prefer the Cosmos Change Feed for guaranteed support.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams; multi-shard change streams are available (preview) and can be enabled via the portal/features; the docs include guidance for enabling cluster-level change streams. Change streams are supported and are the recommended mechanism for online migration and real-time integration (the migration docs rely on change streams).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn 'Change streams in Azure DocumentDB' and migration docs

grounding_links.title: Migrate using online migration (change streams required)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older accounts and other Cosmos DB APIs historically had differing change-notification models; some prior guidance suggested using Cosmos DB Change Feed (SQL API) instead. The vCore DocumentDB offering explicitly provides MongoDB change streams.

confusion_sources.title: Advice to use Cosmos DB Change Feed for change notifications (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable they may design an inefficient polling or workaround approach. The sample can use change streams for live updates or migration validation when desired.
improvements: Add a short note in the migration and quickstart docs clarifying how to enable and use change streams and the portal path to toggle multi-shard change streams (Features → Change streams).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (documentdb profile) for data-plane inspection and tooling for Cosmos DB/Mongo API. The general Azure MCP server does not replace the service-specific documentdb MCP server tooling; use the documentdb profile to inspect collections, indexes and query plans.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools (list DBs, aggregate, create indexes, explain) specific to Azure DocumentDB; the general 'azure' MCP server covers control-plane tasks but not the specialized data-plane commands.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server present) and documentdb-mcp-setup skill

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name/early incarnation of what is now Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure 'DocumentDB' name historically referred to Microsoft’s managed JSON/document database service that evolved and was rebranded to Cosmos DB. It is Microsoft’s proprietary managed service and is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Confusing naming history: the current 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' product was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and was renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB' (the docs note the rename). Separately, the old 'Azure DocumentDB' (2014–2017) became Azure Cosmos DB historically. Also: this new Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation), so it is distinct from the earlier DocumentDB/Cosmos naming and is not Amazon DocumentDB. In short: the cold answer conflates two different historical uses of the 'DocumentDB' name.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn pages 'What is Azure DocumentDB' and release notes

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (naming and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' was used historically by Microsoft and later repurposed when the vCore-based offering emerged; many older pages and blog posts mention 'DocumentDB' → 'Cosmos DB' which introduces ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: Historical rebranding notes and Cosmos/DocumentDB older docs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder confuses which service is meant they may follow the wrong quickstarts or use the wrong resource APIs (databaseAccounts vs mongoClusters).
improvements: Add a small 'Naming FAQ' on the main product page that enumerates (1) original DocumentDB → Cosmos DB (2014–2017), (2) vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB → renamed to Azure DocumentDB, and (3) how to distinguish Amazon DocumentDB and open-source DocumentDB project.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary storage/engine that translates MongoDB wire protocol operations into Cosmos storage operations. For application code you mainly use standard MongoDB drivers, but you must account for service differences (throughput/RU model, some unsupported server features, different consistency/transaction guarantees and query planner behaviors). Expect small compatibility gaps; test your queries against the actual cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore offering) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (hosted project) built on PostgreSQL internals; it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol for driver compatibility. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers, but builders must be aware of platform differences (billing model, some admin commands abstracted) and test against the service. The underlying engine is open-source DocumentDB (not Cosmos DB's earlier internals).
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment skill and Microsoft Learn 'at a glance' pages

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (engine + compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed Cosmos DB internal engine semantics; the vCore product uses the open-source DocumentDB engine, which differs from Cosmos DB's historical engine stack.

confusion_sources.title: Statements describing Cosmos DB internal architecture (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the engine is the Cosmos DB internal stack they may expect RU-idioms or admin commands that don't apply, leading to misconfigured tests or incorrect assumptions about operational behaviour.
improvements: On the main docs, add the sentence: 'This offering is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (PostgreSQL-based) and not on the older Cosmos DB internal store; for drivers, use standard MongoDB drivers.'

confusions.question: What connection string environment variable and exact form will the sample read at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment. Expected form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Do not hard-code credentials; read DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime (or from a .env file) and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient(DOCUMENTDB_URI).
confusions.grounded_answer: The sample should read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment (this is correct). The expected connection string for the vCore DocumentDB offering is typically SRV-style (mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false...), not necessarily the older :10255 port and .mongo.cosmos.azure.com suffix. The sample must accept either SRV or URI provided and pass it directly to MongoClient. Do not hardcode port or host suffix assumptions.
confusions.grounding_source: skill.md (sample prompt) and documentdb-azure-deployment examples
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used older Cosmos DB Mongo API connection string formatting and port; the sample environment and current skill examples use SRV-style hostnames for mongoClusters.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB Mongo connection string examples with port 10255

confusions.build_risk: If the sample rewrites or normalizes DOCUMENTDB_URI to a hardcoded host/port it will break connectivity; the code must accept the env value unchanged.
improvements: In the sample README, add an explicit DOCUMENTDB_URI example placeholder using SRV form and note that both mongodb+srv and mongodb:// forms are accepted verbatim.

confusions.question: Which database name must the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database name sample_customer_360_12 for all collections and operations created/used by this sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment explicitly requires using database sample_customer_360_12 for everything the sample creates.
confusions.grounding_source: sample prompt skill.md

confusions.question: Which Python packages and install command will the sample instruct the developer to install?
confusions.cold_answer: Install the runtime deps with pip. Example: pip install pymongo==4.* langchain openai python-dotenv. (If you use specific vector/embedding libs or the service SDK add them. For agent tools you may add faiss or sentence-transformers only if you run local vector ops — for this sample we rely on DocumentDB vector search so not required.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Reasonable and acceptable: use pymongo (pymongo>=4.x), LangChain, provider SDK (openai or other provider), and python-dotenv. The documentdb-driver skill recommends pymongo and a singleton MongoClient. If the sample uses DocumentDB vector search it does not need local faiss; if the builder chooses an embedding model and local vector ops they must add appropriate libs.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-driver skill and the sample prompt guidance

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will the DocumentDB aggregation tool run to compute purchase frequency, average order value and tenure per customer?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB aggregation pipeline: [ { $match: { status: { $ne: 'cancelled' } } }, { $group: { _id: '$customer_id', orders_count: { $sum: 1 }, total_spent: { $sum: '$order_total' }, avg_order_value: { $avg: '$order_total' }, first_order: { $min: '$order_date' }, last_order: { $max: '$order_date' } } }, { $addFields: { tenure_days: { $dateDiff: { startDate: '$first_order', endDate: '$$NOW', unit: 'day' } }, avg_order_value: '$avg_order_value', orders_count: '$orders_count' } } ]. Run this against the orders collection and join/update against the customers collection as needed.
confusions.grounded_answer: This aggregation pipeline shape is valid on Azure DocumentDB: use $group to compute counts/sums/avgs, $min/$max for first/last order, and $dateDiff (supported) to compute tenure against $$NOW. Joining to customers can be done with $lookup and then an update to the customers collection (updateOne/$set). The natural-language-querying skill can generate and tune this pipeline for the actual sample schema.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-natural-language-querying skill and Microsoft Learn aggregation operators ($dateDiff) docs

confusions.question: What update command will the sample use to write the CLV score, tier and rationale back to the customer profile document?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a standard updateOne call. Example pymongo code: customers.update_one({ '_id': customer_id }, { '$set': { 'clv.score': clv_score, 'clv.tier': clv_tier, 'clv.rationale': clv_rationale, 'clv.updated_at': datetime.utcnow() } }) . Replace customer_id with the document _id. Do not upsert unless you intend to create missing profiles.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: updateOne with $set is the right approach; use the documentdb MCP server's documentdb_find_and_modify or update_documents calls if you need atomic read-modify-write semantics. The sample should avoid upsert by default and set clv.updated_at using the server-side time or client UTC as appropriate.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb MCP server tools and documentdb-driver skill

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters when authoring Bicep/ARM or az resource commands for vCore-based Azure DocumentDB clusters; do not target Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for this product.
Read the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable verbatim and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient; do not assume the host suffix or port (SRV mongodb+srv:// forms are common for mongoClusters).

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the documentdb-specific search and vector APIs: createSearchIndexes + $search (BM25) and cosmosSearch (vector-diskann/vector-hnsw/vector-ivf) rather than MongoDB $text or Atlas-style vector index syntax.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo) and follow the documentdb-driver pattern (singleton MongoClient). For atomic update-and-read you can use findOneAndUpdate / documentdb_find_and_modify via the MCP server; prefer updateOne with $set for simple updates.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (the live cluster exists). If you want to add azd-based dev-to-cloud CI/CD flows, install Azure Developer CLI; otherwise document the manual az/bicep steps. Installation: see Microsoft Learn azd install guide.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Useful if you plan to include an optional IaC path. Install Bicep CLI (az bicep install) or use 'az deployment group create --template-file main.bicep' via az. The documentdb-azure-deployment skill provides a bicep template reference.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Optional for builders who prefer Terraform IaC. Not required for the sample run that uses the existing live cluster. If needed, install Terraform and the AzureRM provider; the documentdb-azure-deployment skill references Terraform templates.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Only needed if building .NET sample variants; not required for this Python LangChain sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Valuable for manual diagnosis. Install mongosh to connect interactively to the cluster when needed; otherwise use the documentdb MCP server tools to inspect data and indexes.
